---
title: "21-scraping: solutions"
---

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(rvest)
library(robotstxt)
```

# Check permission first

```{r}
paths_allowed("https://books.toscrape.com")
paths_allowed("https://quotes.toscrape.com")
paths_allowed("https://www.carleton.edu/catalog/current/search/")
```

All three are `TRUE`, so we're allowed to scrape them. (Remember that `robots.txt` is only part of the story: also check the terms of use, and don't send requests faster than a person would.)

# Part 1: Carleton course catalog

## The STAT listings

```{r}
listings <- read_html("https://www.carleton.edu/catalog/current/search/?subject=STAT&term=26FA")

stat_courses <- tibble(
  course = listings |> html_elements(".courseNumber") |> html_text(),
  title = listings |> html_elements(".courseTitle") |> html_text(),
  credits = listings |> html_elements(".credits") |> html_text() |> str_squish()
)

stat_courses
```

## Missing values

```{r}
length(html_elements(listings, ".courseMeta--preReqs"))

courses <- listings |>
  html_elements(".courseSearchResults > li")

length(courses)
```

1. There are 16 courses but only 14 prerequisite elements. Courses without prerequisites have no `.courseMeta--preReqs` element at all, so they simply disappear from the result, and we can't tell *which* courses they were.
2. `html_element()` (singular), applied to each course, returns one result per course and `NA` when the element is missing:

```{r}
prereqs <- courses |>
  html_element(".courseMeta--preReqs") |>
  html_text() |>
  str_squish()

sum(is.na(prereqs))
```

Two courses have no prerequisites listed.

3. Add `prereqs` to the tibble. (Because every vector now has one entry per course, they line up.)

```{r}
stat_courses <- stat_courses |>
  mutate(prereqs = prereqs)

stat_courses |>
  mutate(prereqs = str_trunc(prereqs, 50))

stat_courses |>
  filter(is.na(prereqs))
```

## Your turn: another department

This example uses Computer Science (`CS`):

```{r}
cs_listings <- read_html("https://www.carleton.edu/catalog/current/search/?subject=CS&term=26FA")

cs_courses <- tibble(
  course = cs_listings |> html_elements(".courseNumber") |> html_text(),
  title = cs_listings |> html_elements(".courseTitle") |> html_text(),
  credits = cs_listings |> html_elements(".credits") |> html_text() |> str_squish() |> parse_number()
)

nrow(cs_courses)

cs_courses |>
  count(credits)
```

Computer Science offers `r nrow(cs_courses)` courses in fall 2026 (the answer depends on the department and term that you choose). Converting `credits` to a number with `parse_number()` lets us summarize it: the maximum is 6 credits and most courses are 6 credits, so "which has the most credits?" has no single answer here.

# Part 2: Books to Scrape

```{r}
books_page <- read_html("https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/page-1.html")

cards <- books_page |>
  html_elements("article.product_pod")

title <- cards |>
  html_element("h3 a") |>
  html_attr("title")

price <- cards |>
  html_element(".price_color") |>
  html_text()

rating <- cards |>
  html_element(".star-rating") |>
  html_attr("class")

books <- tibble(
  title = title,
  price = price,
  rating = rating
)

books |> head()
```

(The title comes from the `title` *attribute* because the displayed text is cut off with "...". The rating is in the *class* of the star element.)

## Clean the data

```{r}
books <- books |>
  mutate(
    price = parse_number(price),
    rating = str_remove(rating, "star-rating "),
    rating = factor(rating, levels = c("One", "Two", "Three", "Four", "Five"))
  )

books |>
  group_by(rating) |>
  summarize(n = n(), mean_price = mean(price))
```

`parse_number()` drops the `£` sign and converts to a number. Making `rating` a factor with the levels in order keeps the ratings from sorting alphabetically (Five, Four, One, ...).

On this one page, the answer to "are the more expensive books rated more highly?" is not clear (only 20 books). With all 1,000 books, it's a clear **no**: average price is about £35 at every rating level, and the correlation between price and rating is about 0.03.

## Many pages

```{r}
scrape_books <- function(page) {
  url <- paste0("https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/page-", page, ".html")
  cards <- read_html(url) |> html_elements("article.product_pod")

  tibble(
    title = cards |> html_element("h3 a") |> html_attr("title"),
    price = cards |> html_element(".price_color") |> html_text() |> parse_number(),
    rating = cards |> html_element(".star-rating") |> html_attr("class") |> str_remove("star-rating "),
    in_stock = cards |> html_element(".availability") |> html_text() |> str_squish() == "In stock",
    page = page
  )
}

books_1_to_3 <- map(1:3, \(p) {
  Sys.sleep(1)
  scrape_books(p)
}) |>
  list_rbind()

nrow(books_1_to_3)
```

Pages 1-3 give 60 books (20 per page). `Sys.sleep(1)` waits a second before each request so that we don't overload the website.

**Challenge:** to count all the books, the same code runs over pages 1 to 50:

```{r}
#| eval: false
all_books <- map(1:50, \(p) {
  Sys.sleep(1)
  scrape_books(p)
}) |>
  list_rbind()

nrow(all_books)
mean(all_books$rating == "Five")
```

There are **1,000 books**, and **196 of them (19.6%)** are rated 5 stars. (This takes about a minute with `Sys.sleep(1)`. Test with a few pages first, and run it once.)

# Part 3: Quotes to Scrape

```{r}
scrape_quotes <- function(page) {
  url <- paste0("https://quotes.toscrape.com/page/", page, "/")
  quotes <- read_html(url) |> html_elements(".quote")

  tibble(
    text = quotes |> html_element(".text") |> html_text(),
    author = quotes |> html_element(".author") |> html_text(),
    tags = quotes |> map_chr(\(q) q |> html_elements(".tag") |> html_text() |> str_c(collapse = ", ")),
    page = page
  )
}

quotes <- scrape_quotes(1)

quotes |>
  mutate(text = str_trunc(text, 40))

quotes |>
  count(author, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(3)
```

Each quote has between 1 and 5 tags, so `html_element(".tag")` (singular) would only get the *first* tag. Instead we select all of the tags inside one quote with `html_elements(".tag")` and combine them with `str_c(collapse = ", ")`. Because `map_chr()` runs this once per quote, we always get exactly one string per quote.

To count the authors, we use `count()`. The most frequent author on page 1 is Albert Einstein (3 quotes).

**Pages 1-3:**

```{r}
quotes_1_to_3 <- map(1:3, \(p) {
  Sys.sleep(1)
  scrape_quotes(p)
}) |>
  list_rbind()

nrow(quotes_1_to_3)

quotes_1_to_3 |>
  count(author, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(3)
```

(An alternative that works for any number of pages: keep following the "Next" button's link, `html_element("li.next a") |> html_attr("href")`, until it is `NA`. Page 10 is the last one.)

# Save your data

The R script `scrape-books.R`:

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(tidyverse)
library(rvest)

scrape_books <- function(page) {
  url <- paste0("https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/page-", page, ".html")
  cards <- read_html(url) |> html_elements("article.product_pod")

  tibble(
    title = cards |> html_element("h3 a") |> html_attr("title"),
    price = cards |> html_element(".price_color") |> html_text() |> parse_number(),
    rating = cards |> html_element(".star-rating") |> html_attr("class") |> str_remove("star-rating "),
    in_stock = cards |> html_element(".availability") |> html_text() |> str_squish() == "In stock",
    page = page
  )
}

books_1_to_3 <- map(1:3, \(p) {
  Sys.sleep(1)
  scrape_books(p)
}) |>
  list_rbind()

write_csv(books_1_to_3, "books.csv")
```

Then, in the .qmd, we read the saved file, so we don't scrape again each time we render:

```{r}
# (here we write to a temporary file so that this document runs on its own)
csv_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
write_csv(books_1_to_3, csv_file)

books_saved <- read_csv(csv_file) |>
  mutate(rating = factor(rating, levels = c("One", "Two", "Three", "Four", "Five")))

ggplot(books_saved, aes(x = rating, y = price)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "Rating", y = "Price (£)", title = "Book prices by rating, pages 1-3")
```

# If a site doesn't allow scraping

```{r}
paths_allowed("https://www.imdb.com/chart/top")
```

Possible alternatives for analyzing IMDb ratings:

- **Use an API.** IMDb has one, but access is cost prohibitive. [The Movie Database (TMDB)](https://www.themoviedb.org/) offers a free API for non-commercial use (with a key), including ratings and popularity.
- **Use a downloadable data set.** For example, a data set that someone has already collected and shared (check the license), or the files that IMDb publishes for personal and non-commercial use.
- **Use a different website** with the same information that allows scraping.
- **Choose a different question**, or a different data set, if the data isn't really necessary.

A tool like {RSelenium} (which controls a real browser) might get around the technical block, but it doesn't change the permission question: if `robots.txt` or the terms of use say no, the answer is still no.
